issues.title: Clarke-subdifferential definition differentiates the wrong function

failure_location.quote:
For a locally Lipschitz continuous function $\phi$, we use $\partial \phi$ to denote its Clarke subdifferential, that is, 
\[
\partial \phi(x) := {\rm conv}\{v : \exists\, x^k \rightarrow x  \text{ such that } \nabla f(x^k) \to v \} \qquad \forall x\in\dom\,\phi.
\]

diagnostic_evidence.quote: When $\phi$ differentiable,  then $\partial \phi$ coincides with the gradient $\nabla \phi$.

issues.failure_explanation: The passage claims to define the Clarke subdifferential of an arbitrary locally Lipschitz function phi, but the displayed defining limits use grad f(x^k). Consequently the displayed set depends on f rather than on phi and is not the asserted Clarke subdifferential.
issues.overall_effect: Read literally, the notation for the Clarke subdifferential is malformed. The surrounding statements and downstream calculations make the intended grad phi reading unambiguous.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace \(\nabla f(x^k)\) by \(\nabla \phi(x^k)\) in the displayed definition of \(\partial\phi(x)\). No argument or downstream statement needs alteration.
issues.why_classification: The passage concerns an arbitrary function \(\phi\), and the immediately following sentence identifies its subdifferential with \(\nabla\phi\) when differentiable. Thus the old source uniquely forces this one-symbol transcriptional correction; the reasoning never uses the erroneous dependence on \(f\).

issues.title: The advertised local-KL example does not satisfy the old Omega-wide condition

failure_location.quote: For example, the minimax problem in Example~\eqref{example} satisfies the local KL condition but not the global one.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the constrained trigonometric problem satisfies the paper's local KL condition. What the example actually establishes is a KL inequality only for feasible x in [1,2]. Any open Omega containing [1,2] also contains positive x outside X; there p is the indicator of [1,2], so the paper's convention gives partial Psi(x) empty and hence an infinite level width. Thus y=pi belongs to the resulting level set, has a positive inner objective gap, and has zero y-residual, contradicting the KL inequality. The material difference is that an inequality on feasible x does not establish the Omega-wide assumption claimed in the remark.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's principal motivating example does not belong to the old stated framework, although the conditional formal theorems are not themselves refuted by this example.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Keep the old \(\Omega\)-wide assumption and revise the remark and related motivating prose to state that the example proves a local KL inequality only for feasible \(x\in[1,2]\), while it is not an instance of Assumption 1(iii) as written. The conditional formal theorems then require no change.
issues.why_classification: The feasible-point inequality and the old \(\Omega\)-wide premise are substantively different, so this is not a transcription error or a no-loss local correction. The stated repair is contained and retains the example's local-versus-global KL phenomenon, but it withdraws the advertised claim that this particular constrained problem belongs to the formal framework. That is a limited, meaningful weakening rather than major loss, so the issue is moderate.

issues.title: The Hölder-smoothness theorem depends on an undeclared gamma parameter
issues.failure_explanation: Theorem thm:Phi_smooth is conditional on Assumption ass:Lip_Smo_KL and states a neighborhood bound involving gamma. The old assumption existentially declares C, theta, and sigma but leaves gamma free in Lev_set. Moreover, zero or negative gamma cannot supply the positive level width, trust-region radius, and inverse powers used later. Thus the theorem's parameter regime is not well-defined as written.
issues.overall_effect: The local level set, Hölder neighborhood, outer step radius, subsolver level parameter, and gamma-dependent complexity constants lack a declared admissible parameter throughout the main formal chain.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Amend Assumption 1(iii) to declare that there exist \(C>0\), \(\theta\in[1/2,1)\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(\sigma>0\), using that same \(\gamma\) in the level set, algorithm, and complexity constants.
issues.why_classification: The old algorithm and later statements explicitly say that \(\gamma\) comes from the assumption, while the positive level width, ball radius, and inverse powers uniquely force \(\gamma>0\). The symbol is simply omitted from the parameter declaration; adding it repairs the malformed binder throughout the chain without changing any inference or guarantee.

issues.title: The main stationarity guarantee invokes a definition outside its declared scope

failure_location.quote: $x^k$ is an $(\epsilon, \gamma \epsilon^\sigma/(4L_f))$-stationary point of problem~\eqref{intro_problem} (or equivalently the problem $\min_x \Psi(x)$)

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Suppose $\phi$ is a locally Lipschitz continuous function.

issues.failure_explanation: The old definition introduces an (epsilon,r)-stationary point only for a locally Lipschitz function phi. Assumption ass:Lip_Smo_KL permits a proper closed convex p taking the value +infinity, and Psi=F*+p therefore need not be a locally Lipschitz real-valued function; the paper's own constrained numerical model uses indicator terms. Consequently, thm:outer_bound applies its declared stationarity notion to objectives not covered by that definition.
issues.overall_effect: For the allowed constrained and indicator-valued models, the main iteration and oracle guarantees use an approximate-stationarity contract whose stated domain does not include the objective being analyzed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Extend the approximate-stationarity definition to proper closed extended-real-valued objectives: use the limiting subdifferential, set \(\mathcal S_\epsilon=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}\phi:\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\phi(x))\leq\epsilon\}\), and retain the old distance-to-\(\mathcal S_\epsilon\) definition of an \((\epsilon,r)\)-stationary point. State that \(\Psi=F^*+p\) is proper closed and interpret both complexity theorems under this definition.
issues.why_classification: This is a genuine scope defect because the old definition expressly covers only locally Lipschitz real-valued functions. Nevertheless, the proof already targets distance to the subgradient-critical set of the composite objective, and the standard extended-valued definition makes that contract valid for indicator constraints without changing the algorithm, stationarity tolerance, rates, model class, or conclusions. The required repair is short and routine, so it is minor rather than moderate or serious.

issues.title: The openness lemma omits the regularity needed for its exact sum rule

failure_location.quote: By this and $\Psi=F^*+p$, one has $\partial \Psi=\partial F^*+\partial p$ on $\cX$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: It is also well-known that $\partial (\phi_1 + \phi_2)(x) = \nabla \phi_1(x) + \partial \phi_2(x)$ if $\phi_1$ is differentiable and $\phi_2$ is locally Lipschitz continuous at $x$

issues.failure_explanation: The old proof needs the exact identity partial Psi=partial F*+partial p in order to pass bounded subgradients to a limit. Lemma lem:Lips only gives Lipschitz continuity of F*, and the paper's previously stated sum rule requires differentiability of the smooth summand and local Lipschitz continuity of the other summand—conditions not established here for F* and the extended-valued p. The existing smoothness assumptions can instead be used to prove that F* is weakly convex, after which a convex sum rule gives the needed identity; that argument is absent in version 1.
issues.overall_effect: Without the missing subdifferential-calculus step, closedness of the bounded-subgradient set and hence openness of U_epsilon are not established; the differentiability extension and the outer complexity proof depend on that property.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Insert the missing subdifferential-calculus argument in Lemma lem:open: smoothness of every \(f(\cdot,y)\) implies weak convexity of \(F^*\); after quadratic convexification, the qualified convex sum rule with convex \(p\) yields \(\partial\Psi=\partial F^*+\partial p\) on \(\mathcal X\). Then decompose each bounded \(s^k\in\partial\Psi(x^k)\), use the local boundedness of \(\partial F^*\), and pass to limits by outer semicontinuity to prove the required closedness and openness.
issues.why_classification: The old invocation of the exact sum rule is invalid, so this is not a typo. However, all needed regularity is already supplied by the stated smoothness and convexity assumptions, and the repair is a standard, local weak-convexity and sum-rule argument. It preserves Lemma lem:open and every listed dependent result with unchanged hypotheses, conclusions, and complexity guarantees, requiring no new proof architecture.

issues.title: The stationary-set typo invalidates the subsolver-output lemma

diagnostic_evidence.quote: By the assumption in this lemma, we know that $x^0\in \cX^\rc_\epsilon$ and hence $\dist(0, \partial \Psi(x^0)) > \epsilon$.

issues.failure_explanation: The old equation defines X_epsilon using dist(0,Psi(x)), a scalar objective-value test. In lem:subsolver_output, membership in the corresponding X_epsilon complement is used to infer dist(0,partial Psi(x))>epsilon and hence to invoke the local KL condition. A point can be stationary while its objective value is far from zero, so the inference does not follow from the old definition.
issues.overall_effect: The old proof cannot place the relevant iterates and line segments in U_epsilon, so the local KL subsolver guarantee, descent argument, and final iteration and oracle bounds are not established from the displayed definitions.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\) by \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial\Psi(x))\) in the definition of \(\mathcal X_\epsilon\) and in the matching copied prose. The complement then has exactly the stationarity meaning used in the subsolver and outer proofs.
issues.why_classification: The earlier definition of approximate stationarity, the set \(\mathcal U_\epsilon\), and every subsequent use of \(\mathcal X_\epsilon\) uniquely require the subgradient residual. The scalar objective-value interpretation is never used by the reasoning. Restoring the omitted \(\partial\) symbol therefore corrects a transcriptional definition error without repairing any mathematical argument or changing any guarantee.
